newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says U.S. helping anti-Saddam Iraqis flee.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says U.S. helping anti-Saddam Iraqis flee.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Monday the United States is helping "those who have worked with us" to flee Iraq amid Kurdish strife that reportedly wrecked a CIA effort to topple Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
"We're doing everything we think we can to help anyone who needs to be out of Iraq," Clinton told reporters.

He declined to elaborate, but he was responding to a question about some 200 Iraqi Arabs with links to the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency who reportedly fled the Kurdish city of Arbil after Iraqi troops stormed it last week.
The Iraqi intervention prompted U.S. retaliation in the form of cruise missile strikes against anti-aircraft defences and expansion of a no-fly zone in the south of Iraq.

The Washington Post reported on Monday that the Kurdish opponents of Saddam in the Arbil region, all of whom belong to the U.S.-financed Iraqi National Congress, are holed up in a mountain hideout in northern Iraq fearing for their lives and hoping for U.S. political asylum.
About 100 of their colleagues were arrested by Iraqi secret police and apparently executed after Arbil was overrun, the Post said, quoting U.S. officials and Iraqi dissidents.

"We're doing everything we can to get out of Iraq American citizens and those who have worked with us," Clinton said. "As to the intelligence matters, I can't comment, but we are doing everything that we can do and we believe is appropriate."
Clinton said the fighting in northern Iraq, which brought Baghdad's intervention and the U.S. retaliation to it last week, was once again confined primarily to Kurdish factions.

The United States, which unsuccessfully tried to broker power-sharing agreement among the warring Kurds, has warned them against "any cavalier killing" of civilians or other non-combatants, the president said.

There have been published reports that Clinton expanded the covert anti-Saddam operation in January, signing a secret order directing the CIA to provide weapons and training and to install intelligence-gathering equipment for Saddam's foes.

But Iraq's military thrust into what had been a Kurdish safe haven effectively destroyed the cloak-and-dagger operation and caused a handful of CIA agents to flee the area, the Post and other newspapers said.

U.S. Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said after addressing the Southern Governors' Conference in Kansas City on Sunday that he was concerned, and would seek a report from the Senate Intelligence Committee.

"I want to know what the circumstances were for their (CIA operatives) being withdrawn," Lott told Reuters. "What did we do to those that were working with us? Did we expose them to what has now been their apparent execution? I'm not condemning it, I just want to know what the deal is."

The CIA declined comment on the setback to its long-standing effort to oust Saddam, said by experts to be the biggest U.S. covert operation since aiding guerrillas opposed to Soviet troops in Afghanistan in the 1980s.

Lee Hamilton, the senior Democratic member of the House of Representatives International Relations committee, said the United States had been working with "all kinds of groups that we think are dissidents" as part of the covert campaign.
"We've financed it. We've done some military training. We've provided some intelligence," he said in an interview on Fox television on Sunday.
Helping rescue Kurds who worked with the CIA would normally be a high priority for operational reasons as well as for moral ones, experts said.

"They don't want these guys to be captured and tortured" for fear they would disclose more secrets, said Kenneth Katzman, a former CIA analyst who tracks Iraq and Iran at the Congressional Research Service.
